# naveed.io — Naveed Kakal

> Naveed Kakal is Lead Developer at Kannegiesser ETECH and an electrical engineer. For
> twenty years he has written code in every layer of the software that runs industrial laundry
> plants, among the hardest material handling there is: plant layout with sales,
> generated PLC programs, the eVue plant control system (the role a WCS/WES plays in a
> warehouse, or an MES in a factory), labor tracking and productivity, plant reporting,
> a share of the cloud reporting that spans 400+ plants, and the Pulse mobile app.
> He works on a very small team with projects on several continents, which is how he came
> to understand the whole plant end to end and to know its customers first-hand. The same stack
> applies to warehouses, factories and airports: sensors, controllers, routing and
> reports, with different nouns. Since 2025 he also builds with a fleet of AI agents
> (10,402 commits across 103 repositories in the year to October 2026).
> This site is his dossier: case files and field notes drawn from recorded interviews
> and 10,134 commits of version-control history (March 2009 – September 2026) on one
> product line — 3,209 in Subversion (2009–2014) and 6,925 in git (2017–present).

## The stack he has built, bottom up

- L0 The plan: plant layout with the sales team (the controls gotchas, what the
  system can and can't do) and the product's long-term roadmap.
- L1 I/O and field devices: photo-eyes, proximity switches, scales, motor drives. One
  plant he supports maps 8,710 I/O points into a single controller. Click-to-force, a
  commissioning test tool, has been his testing standard since early 2009; paired with
  a test PLC, it exercises the full stack before a real item moves.
- L2 Machine control: PLC programs generated from each plant's database (129 device
  types, 123 B&R PLCs), replacing hand-written programs. PLC communications via SOAP
  (2007), an Elixir service (2019) and an OPC UA bridge today. Rule: never act on a
  stale sensor.
- L3 Screens and workflows: eVue, a web-based plant control system since 2007 (Rails,
  React), never rewritten; routing, storage, sort stations, autopilot for what goes
  next, plain-language alarms, configured per plant workflow. One plant: 611 rail
  sections and 93 machines.
- L4 People and productivity: operator logins by station and task, piece-rate and team
  pounds-per-operator-hour measures, breaks and shifts, supervisor reports.
- L5 Local reporting: KPI dashboards and scheduled reports on the plant's own server,
  so the floor runs when the internet doesn't.
- L6 Cloud reporting: a hub at every site rolls numbers up every minute across 400+
  plants. A team build: teammates Jason and Larry did most of it; Naveed contributed.
- L7 Mobile: Pulse, a phone app that gets plant data securely off isolated plant
  networks to supervisors (QR-linked devices, push alerts).

## Timeline

- 1997–2006: Worked at and eventually managed Royal Oaks Car Wash, Shoreview, Minnesota.
- August 2006: Hired at ETECH (Minneapolis) onto the controls team, on the GE 90-30 /
  Cimplicity predecessor system.
- March 2009: First commit on the record ("sorting is working?"); the new web-based
  platform's click-to-force testing starts here (r361, "Working on force").
- Fall 2009: Commissioned the new platform at Angelica's Los Angeles plant.
- 2012: The Ottawa incident — a production database dropped at a running plant; the
  customer stayed for fourteen years.
- September 2014 – February 2017: Centro, Chicago — developer, then dev lead and
  engineering manager.
- March 2017: Returned to ETECH, just as Kannegiesser acquired the company, as Cathay
  Pacific's Vogue Laundry in Hong Kong (then ETECH's largest project) was commissioning.
- December 2018: First Hong Kong trip — Wireshark captures that helped trace a network
  broadcast storm to a saturated switch trunk.
- October 2019: PLC communications moved to an Elixir application he started that April.
- November 2025: 434 commits in one month.
- August 2026: 10,000th commit on the record.
- October 2026: On site in Hong Kong for Vogue's eVue 5 → v26 upgrade (layout, PLC,
  network and fiber work included); 36-hour window, most of the system running in under 20.
- Today: Lead Developer, Kannegiesser ETECH; 400+ plants run eVue.

## Working principles

From the case files, in his words where possible:

1. Count problems solved per developer dollar.
2. Remove the seams — responsibility leaks out through the joints between specialists.
3. Speak the floor's language — use the operators' words, so the floor can tell when the
   software is wrong.
4. Let reality win — when the plant and its digital picture drift, ask a human what
   happened, and offer only answers that can physically occur.
5. Trust is the infrastructure.
6. Improve the condemned — a dying system's real limits become its successor's spec.

## Method

The writing on this site is produced through a human-AI pipeline Naveed built himself:
an interview skill for Claude Code researches his ~19 years of version-control history
for verifiable facts, interviews him one question at a time (he answers by voice), and
drafts each piece in a chosen style — the styles rotate across the series. Naveed
fact-checks every number and edits every draft before publication. The pipeline is
itself a demonstration of the subject matter: applied judgment about what AI tooling is
for. Each article's JSON-LD declares the interview basis (`isBasedOn`), the style
(`genre`), and the AI contributor (`contributor`).

## Writing — On record

- [Arguing with your own legacy](https://naveed.io/writing/arguing-with-your-own-legacy.html):
  Case file on Cathay Pacific's Vogue Laundry in Hong Kong (eVue job 2326), ETECH's largest
  project when it was commissioned in 2017. The 2018 broadcast storm (I/O controllers
  missing inputs, a misrouted track switch becoming a jam cleared from lifts), traced via
  Wireshark to a saturated 1 Gb trunk and relieved short-term by slowing the server's port
  to 100 Mbps — a colleague's fix, his data. Nine years on eVue 5 made it the operators'
  "correct" way; the October 2026 upgrade to eVue v26 meant holding the line on new
  workflows (automated recirculation) instead of rebuilding old ones — "I have done 400 of
  these laundries… let me come and make you feel safe and taken care of" — plus PLC,
  switch and fiber upgrades in a 36-hour window, most of it running in under 20.

- [The prank that brought him back](https://naveed.io/writing/prank-that-brought-him-back.html):
  Case file on the 2014–2017 gap. Why he left after eight years (the "does my
  experience translate?" itch), the Centro years in Chicago tech — becoming a better
  developer, watching thoughtful projects become "a flotilla of blah," discovering he's
  an IC at heart who was promoted to dev lead and engineering manager anyway — and the
  fake service call prank that reconnected him with ETECH, weeks before learning
  Kannegiesser had acquired the company. Returned March 2017, "better armed and less
  scared," and reshaped the department into a product team.

- [Teaching the condemned new tricks](https://naveed.io/writing/teaching-the-condemned.html):
  Case file on the 2006–2009 prehistory, before version control saw him. Hired off a
  car-wash hunch by Brian Schlichting; the GE 90-30/Cimplicity era and its per-seat
  licensing villain; improving a condemned system as R&D for its successor; the
  click-to-force testing concept that crossed into the new platform (r361, "Working on
  force," March 2009) and still lives in its simulator tools; the Angelica LA
  commissioning (slept in cars); trust as the infrastructure under bespoke systems.

- [Seventeen years in the same problem](https://naveed.io/writing/seventeen-years-same-problem.html):
  Case file on concentrated experience. The plant as a physical database (sling + rail
  as the two god models), inventory drift and its human repair workflows, the 2012
  Ottawa incident (a production database dropped at a running plant, and the trust-first
  recovery that kept the customer for fourteen years), problems-solved-per-developer-dollar,
  and why AI-era teams are converging on the fewer-seams, one-capable-person shape.
